lines.text: Now the reaction time: zero point zero five seconds.
Readings are a little old, and each command waits for the loop, then travels over the CAN wires.
Meanwhile it keeps rolling: at four meters per second, zero point two meters.
So it subtracts speed times zero point zero five from the distance first.
From top speed, braking now starts at one point five three meters, not one point three three.
Next, the gentle line: speed equals K P, a gain of six, times distance.
Where does it cross the braking curve? Where six d equals the square root of twelve d.
Square both sides: thirty-six d squared equals twelve d. So d is a third of a meter, at two meters per second.
Closer than that, the line is lower, so it wins.
Why bother? Near zero, the curve is almost vertical.
One millimeter out, the curve asks for eleven centimeters per second. The line, under one.
Measured positions always wiggle. A steep curve turns every wiggle into a lurch.
In our simulator, with a centimeter of noise, the curve alone jittered about nine centimeters per second.
A K P of eight or more also wobbled at the finish. Six didn't.
Last: inside three millimeters, the stop deadband sets speed to exactly zero.
